**You are entitled to at least 12 days of paid annual leave each year after 3 years of work.**

**What the law says**
Under the law, an employee gets "twelve days for every twelve months of continuous service" (working for the same employer without a break) if employed for 2 years or more but less than 5 years (Employment Act 1955, s.60E(1)(b)).

**What could change this**
- **Your employment contract:** Your contract can grant more leave, but cannot give you less than the statutory minimum (Employment Act 1955, s.7).
- **Your location:** The Employment Act 1955 applies in Peninsular Malaysia and the Federal Territory of Labuan (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)). Sabah and Sarawak fall under separate Labour Ordinances.
- **Unpaid leave:** If you took unpaid leave exceeding 30 days in a 12-month period, that time is excluded when calculating your length of service (Employment Act 1955, s.60E(3b)).
- **Unexcused absence:** You lose entitlement to that leave if you were absent without permission or reasonable excuse for more than 10% of working days in that year (Employment Act 1955, s.60E(1)).

Please verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my, as statutory amendments may have taken place.

**Your employer must give you the notice period specified in your employment contract, or the legal minimum notice based on how long you have worked there if your contract does not state one.**

**What the law says**
The notice length must be identical for both employer and employee and is determined by a written contract. In the absence of a written agreement, the notice "shall not be less than":
* 4 weeks if employed for less than 2 years;
* 6 weeks if employed for 2 years or more but less than 5 years;
* 8 weeks if employed for 5 years or more (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)).

**What could change this**
* **Written contract terms**: A written clause in your contract of service (employment agreement) sets the required notice length (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)).
* **Length of service**: If your contract is silent, your required notice increases after 2 and 5 years of service (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)).
* **Waiver**: Either party may choose to waive (give up) the right to notice (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)).
* **Location**: The Employment Act 1955 applies to Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan; Sabah and Sarawak are governed by separate state labour enactments (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)).

**You are entitled to at least 98 consecutive days of maternity leave for each childbirth.**

**What the law says**
Under the law, maternity leave lasts for an eligible period of "not less than ninety-eight consecutive days" for each confinement (giving birth after at least 22 weeks of pregnancy) (Employment Act 1955, s.37(1)(a)(i), s.37(1)(d)(ii)).

**What could change this**
- **Pay during leave:** You receive maternity allowance (full pay during leave) only if you worked for your employer for at least 90 days in the 9 months before giving birth, and worked at any time in the 4 months before giving birth (Employment Act 1955, s.37(2)(a)).
- **Number of children:** You do not receive paid leave if you already have 5 or more surviving natural children at the time of birth (Employment Act 1955, s.37(1)(c), s.37(1)(d)(i)).
- **Location:** This Act applies only in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)). Sabah and Sarawak are covered by separate labour laws not included here.
- **Timing:** Leave cannot start earlier than 30 days before birth or later than the day right after birth (Employment Act 1955, s.37(1)(b)).

You can verify the latest text at lom.agc.gov.my.

**You are entitled to between 14 and 22 days of paid sick leave per calendar year if you do not need hospital care, depending on how long you have worked for your employer. If you need hospitalization (staying in a hospital for medical treatment), you are entitled to 60 days in total per calendar year.**

**What the law says**
Under (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1)(aa)), where no hospitalization is needed, you get:
- 14 days if employed for less than 2 years;
- 18 days if employed for 2 years or more but less than 5 years;
- 22 days if employed for 5 years or more.

If hospitalization is needed, you get "sixty days in the aggregate in each calendar year" (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(1)(bb)). You count as hospitalized if a doctor certifies you are ill enough to need hospital care even if not admitted.

**What could change this**
- Your length of service (how long you have worked for the same employer).
- Whether a registered doctor or dental surgeon certifies your illness.
- Informing your employer within 48 hours of the leave starting (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(2)(b)).
- Whether your employment contract gives you more generous benefits (Employment Act 1955, s.7).
- Whether you are currently on maternity leave or receiving disablement compensation (Employment Act 1955, s.60F(4)).
- Location, as this statute applies to Peninsular Malaysia (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)).

**An employer in the private sector cannot force you to retire before you reach 60 years old.**

**What the law says**
The minimum retirement age is 60 years old, and an employer must not prematurely retire (force an employee to retire before the legal age) an employee before that age (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.4(1), s.5(1)). Any clause in an employment agreement that sets an earlier retirement age is "deemed to be void and substituted with the minimum retirement age" (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.7(1)).

**What could change this**
* **Optional retirement:** You can choose to retire earlier if your contract or collective agreement (a contract between an employer and a trade union) allows it (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, s.6).
* **Excluded workers:** The 60-year rule does not apply to probationers, non-citizen employees, domestic workers, or fixed-term contract staff on terms of 24 months or less (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, Schedule).
* **Public sector:** Employees paid by the government, statutory bodies, or local authorities fall under separate public sector laws (Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012, Schedule; Pensions Act 1980, s.10).

**A trade union gets recognised by serving a written claim on an employer, who must reply within 21 days by either granting recognition or stating why it is refused. If the employer refuses or does not reply, the union can refer the matter to the Director General for Industrial Relations, who can decide to grant recognition.**

### What the law says
- **Serving the claim:** A registered trade union of workmen serves a written claim for recognition (a formal legal request to represent workers in negotiations) on the employer (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(2)).
- **Employer's response:** The employer must respond within 21 days to either accord recognition or state written grounds for refusal (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(3)). 
- **Director General's decision:** If the employer refuses or fails to reply, the union has 14 days to report this in writing to the Director General (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(4)). The Director General may hold a secret ballot (a confidential vote among workers) to check support and make a binding decision (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(4A), s.9(5)). If approved, recognition is *"deemed to be accorded by the employer"* from a specified date (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(5)).

### What could change this
- **Job category:** General unions cannot seek recognition for workers employed in a managerial, executive, confidential, or security capacity (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(1)).
- **Missed deadlines:** If the union does not report an employer's refusal or silence to the Director General within 14 days, the claim is treated as withdrawn (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.9(4)).
- **Existing claims or recognition:** Another union cannot make a claim for the same group of workers while a claim is pending or within the waiting period after recognition is given (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.10A, s.11).

*This covers federal principal Acts only; verify the latest text at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Yes, anyone who runs a business of lending money in Malaysia must have a valid licence.**

**What the law says:**
Under (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.5(1)), no person may carry on or advertise that they carry on the business of moneylending (lending money at interest) unless they are licensed. Carrying on business without a licence is an offence carrying a fine between RM250,000 and RM1,000,000, imprisonment for up to 5 years, or both (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.5(2)).

**What could change this:**
- **Specific exempt bodies**: The licensing requirement does not apply to entities listed in the First Schedule, such as licensed banks (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.2A(1)).
- **Ministerial exemptions**: The Minister may specifically exempt a company or society through a notice in the Gazette (an official government publication) (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.2A(2)).
- **Non-business lending**: Occasional lending between private individuals without running a business does not fall under the definition of a moneylender (Moneylenders Act 1951, s.2).

*Note: This covers federal principal Acts only and does not include case law or subsidiary legislation. Please verify the current law at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Generally no, a company cannot process your personal data without your consent. However, the law allows them to do so in specific situations, such as when fulfilling a contract with you or complying with a legal duty.**

**What the law says**
Under the General Principle (Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.6(1)(a)), a data user (a business or person that handles personal information) must not process your data unless you, the data subject (the individual the data is about), have given consent. 

Even so, a company may process your personal data without your consent if it is necessary to (Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.6(2)):
- perform a contract you are part of, or take steps at your request to enter into a contract;
- comply with any legal obligation (other than a contract);
- protect your vital interests;
- administer justice; or
- carry out functions under any written law.

**What could change this**
- **Commercial context:** The law only applies to commercial transactions (business dealings, goods, or services).
- **Exemptions:** Consent is not needed for specific statutory exemptions, such as crime investigations or court orders (Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.45).
- **Sensitive data:** If the information is sensitive personal data (such as your health or political opinions), stricter rules apply (Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s.40).

*Note: Federal Acts are consolidated snapshots. Verify the current text at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**As a company director, you must always act honestly in the best interests of the company, and you must carry out your work with reasonable care, skill, and diligence.**

### What the law says
- **Loyalty and purpose:** You must exercise your powers "for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company" (Companies Act 2016, s.213(1)).
- **Care and skill:** You must exercise reasonable care, skill, and diligence based on what is reasonably expected of your role, plus any extra knowledge or skill you actually have (Companies Act 2016, s.213(2)).
- **No improper use:** You must not use company property, inside information, your position, or business opportunities to gain a personal benefit or harm the company without member approval at a general meeting (a formal meeting of company shareholders) (Companies Act 2016, s.218(1)).
- **Nominee directors:** If you are a nominee director (appointed to represent a specific shareholder or employer), you cannot place that person's interests ahead of the company's interests (Companies Act 2016, s.217(1)).

### What could change this
- **Business judgments:** You are treated as meeting your duty of care if you made a business judgment (a commercial decision to act or not act) in good faith, with no personal interest, and with appropriate information (Companies Act 2016, s.214(1)).
- **Relying on others:** You may rely on reports or advice from qualified officers or experts if you do so in good faith and after your own independent assessment (Companies Act 2016, s.215).
- **Company constitution:** Specific internal powers and board procedures can be modified by the company constitution (internal company rules) (Companies Act 2016, s.211(2)).

*This covers federal principal Acts only and does not include case law. Verify current legislation at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Compensation is based primarily on the market value (the price the land would sell for between a willing buyer and seller) of your land at the date of the formal acquisition notice, plus compensation for certain specific financial losses.**

**What the law says**
Under (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.2), the Land Administrator (the district officer in charge of land matters) must consider only:
- The market value of the land at the official notice date (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.1(1), s.2(a)).
- Damage caused by severing (cutting off) the acquired portion from your remaining land (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.2(c)).
- Damage injuriously affecting (harming the use or value of) your other movable or immovable property (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.2(d)).
- Reasonable moving expenses if you must change your home or business location (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.2(e)).

Your unwillingness to sell and the urgency of the acquisition cannot be considered (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.3). You cannot be awarded more than the amount you claimed at the inquiry (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.4(a)).

**What could change this**
- Whether the government takes your entire plot or only a part of it (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.1(1B)).
- Title restrictions (conditions written on the title limiting how the land may be used) or local zoning plans (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.1(2), s.1(2BA)).
- Whether the land is Malay reservation land or customary land (Land Acquisition Act 1960, First Schedule, s.1(2A)).
- State land enactments, case law, or valuation guidelines, which are outside this federal principal Acts corpus.

**What the law says**  
The law empowers the Minister of Human Resources to set minimum wage rates by publishing a "minimum wages order" in the Gazette (National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, s.23(1)). If the rate in your contract of service (employment agreement) is lower than the rate in the order, it must be substituted with the minimum wage rate (National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, s.24(2)).

**What could change this**  
* The specific rate depends on the latest Minimum Wages Order, which is subsidiary legislation not included in this database of principal Acts.  
* The Minister may set different rates or starting dates for different regions, sectors, or types of work (National Wages Consultative Council Act 2011, s.22(1)).  

To find the current minimum wage rate, please check the latest Minimum Wages Order at lom.agc.gov.my.

**Your employer must pay a statutory monthly contribution to your EPF based on your monthly wage bracket, calculated according to the rates set out in the Third Schedule.**

### What the law says
Under (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.45(1)), the employer is liable in the first instance to pay *"both the contributions payable by himself and also, on behalf of and to the exclusion of the employee"*. The employer is legally prohibited from deducting the employer's share from your wages or remuneration (payment for work done) (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.47(1)).

### What could change this
- **Your monthly wages:** The exact dollar amount your employer must contribute is tiered based on your wage bracket in the Third Schedule.
- **Your age:** Different contribution rates apply if you reach 60 years of age (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, Third Schedule, Part C & Part D).
- **Your citizenship status:** Specific rules and separate schedules apply to Malaysian citizens, permanent residents, and non-citizens (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, Third Schedule, Part C & Part D).
- **Voluntary excess contributions:** An employer or employee can elect to contribute at a higher rate than the statutory schedule (Employees Provident Fund Act 1991, s.43(3)).

*Note: EPF contribution rates in principal Acts are consolidated snapshots and can be amended by subsidiary legislation (such as ministerial orders). Please verify the current figures at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Yes, you are generally covered if you are an insured employee injured while travelling to work. The law treats this as an employment injury (a work-related injury), as long as you were on your direct route and did not make personal detours.**

### What the law says
Under the law, an accident that occurs while travelling on a route between your place of residence and your workplace is treated as happening in the course of your employment (Employees’ Social Security Act 1969, s.24(1)). However, if the accident occurs during any *"interruption of, or deviation from"* your journey, it will not be treated as a work injury (Employees’ Social Security Act 1969, s.24(2)).

### What could change this
* **Detours or breaks:** You lose coverage for that trip if you deviated from your usual route or stopped for personal reasons not related to your job (Employees’ Social Security Act 1969, s.24(2)).
* **Registration and contributions:** You must qualify as an insured person (an employee for whom social security contributions are payable) (Employees’ Social Security Act 1969, s.2(11)).
* **Excluded jobs:** Certain individuals, such as casual workers employed outside an employer's regular business, police officers, or military personnel, fall outside standard coverage (Employees’ Social Security Act 1969, s.3).
* **Self-employment:** If you work for yourself rather than under an employment contract, travelling coverage falls under separate rules (Self-Employment Social Security Act 2017, s.3).

*This text reflects consolidated federal statutes only. Always verify current statutory provisions at [lom.agc.gov.my](https://lom.agc.gov.my).*

**Under Malaysian law, only written documents (known as instruments) specifically listed in the First Schedule to the Stamp Act 1949 are chargeable with stamp duty.**

**What the law says**
Under the Stamp Act 1949, First Schedule (read with section 33 and the Third Schedule), the main documents subject to stamp duty include:
- **Agreements and contracts**.
- **Conveyances** (transfers of property ownership, gifts, or company shares).
- **Charges and mortgages** (documents giving a lender security rights over property), debentures, bonds, and loan or financing agreements.
- **Leases and tenancy agreements** for land or buildings.
- **Deeds, declarations of trust, letters of guarantee, and insurance policies**.

**What could change this**
- **Statutory exemptions:** Some documents are legally exempt, such as employment contracts for wages of RM300 or less per month, ordinary goods sales agreements that are not hire-purchase, and documents executed by or for the Government (Stamp Act 1949, s.1 [Section 35] and First Schedule, Item 4).
- **Oral agreements:** Stamp duty applies to written instruments, not unwritten verbal arrangements.
- **Location of execution:** A document executed outside Malaysia is generally chargeable within 30 days after it is first received in Malaysia (Stamp Act 1949, s.42(1)).

*Note: This text is from a consolidated snapshot of the Act and may not reflect recent amendments. Please verify the current law at lom.agc.gov.my.*

**Two weeks of notice is not enough under standard statutory minimums, which require at least 4 weeks. Whether it is valid depends on your length of service, your written contract, and whether you receive payment in place of notice.**

**What the law says**
Notice length is set by your contract of service (an employment agreement), but if the contract does not specify a period, notice "shall not be less than" 4 weeks for under 2 years of service, 6 weeks for 2 to 5 years, and 8 weeks for 5 years or more (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)). A contract term less favourable to you than the Act is void (Employment Act 1955, s.7). An employer may end employment earlier by paying an indemnity (payment instead of notice) equal to your wages for the unexpired notice (Employment Act 1955, s.13(1)), or dismiss without notice for misconduct after due inquiry (Employment Act 1955, s.14(1)(a)).

**What could change this**
- **Length of service:** Minimum notice is 4, 6, or 8 weeks depending on your years with the employer (Employment Act 1955, s.12(2)).
- **Payment in lieu:** An employer can give 2 weeks of working notice if they pay wages for the rest of the required notice period (Employment Act 1955, s.13(1)).
- **Location:** The Employment Act 1955 applies in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan (Employment Act 1955, s.1(2)); Sabah and Sarawak are governed by separate state labour laws not included in this corpus.

**No, an employer cannot lawfully dismiss you without a proper reason.**

**What the law says:**
A workman (a person employed under a contract of employment) who considers they were "dismissed without just cause or excuse" (without a valid, fair legal reason) may challenge the dismissal (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.20(1)). In addition, for misconduct (improper behavior at work), an employer may only dismiss you "on the grounds of misconduct inconsistent with the fulfilment of the express or implied conditions of his service, after due inquiry" (Employment Act 1955, s.14(1)).

**What could change this:**
- Whether your position qualifies as a workman under the Act (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.2).
- Whether the employer terminated the contract with notice or indemnity (wages paid in place of notice) under standard contract terms (Employment Act 1955, s.12, s.13(1)), though a dismissal still requires just cause.
- Missing the filing deadline: any challenge must be filed within 60 days of the dismissal (Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.20(1A)).

**To register a trade union, you must submit a formal application to the Director General of Trade Unions within 6 months of establishing the union.**

### What the law says
* **Deadline:** A new union must apply for registration within 6 months from the date it is established (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.8(1)).
* **Application requirements:** The application must be in the prescribed form and *"signed by at least seven members of the union"* (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.10(1)). 
* **Required attachments:** You must include the prescribed fee, a printed copy of the union's rules in the national language (Malay) signed by the applicants, and details of the applicants, union name, registered head office, and union officers (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.10(2)).
* **Certificate:** Once registered, the Director General issues a certificate of registration (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.13).

### What could change this
* **Time extensions:** The Director General may grant an extension of time to apply, up to a maximum total of 12 months (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.8(2)).
* **Requests for more details:** The Director General has the power to demand additional information before deciding on the application (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.14).
* **Member eligibility:** Certain categories of workers, such as police, armed forces, or public officers (civil servants), have statutory limits or prohibitions on joining or forming trade unions (Trade Unions Act 1959, s.27).

*Note: Specific application forms, procedures, and fees are governed by subsidiary regulations. For consequential matters, verify current text at lom.agc.gov.my.*
